parts.text: This is the official portfolio and creative hub of Calvin McWilliams — UX/UI designer, UX engineer, web developer, and multi-disciplinary creative. Calvin designs and builds intentional digital systems where aesthetics, functionality, and human behavior align to create clear, intuitive experiences. He specializes in crafting high-impact solutions that balance visual design, usability, and user psychology.

Backed by a Google UX Design Certification, I specialize in creating user-centered experiences for web and mobile platforms. My process is driven by in-depth UX research, usability testing, and iterative prototyping, ensuring designs are both functional and engaging.

I design and engineer responsive web experiences using HTML5, CSS, JavaScript, Google Apps Script, and React. Grounded in UX principles and accessibility standards, I translate product logic and human behavior into clear, intuitive interfaces.

With six years of independent UX and web design experience, four years at Accenture, and contract work with AMD, I bring a broad talent stack that bridges user experience, design, and front-end development.

caseStudy.title: SpeedRun-X (name changed to protect AMD's IP)

sections.heading: Problem
body: The existing workflow orchestration system had no clear starting point, no defined progression, and no reliable sense of what should happen next. Users were simply required to hold too much of the system in their heads at once and critical actions like configuring workloads or assigning environments were buried in inconsistent locations. The system exposed nearly all of its complexity upfront. With many of the users having little to no background in engineering, this created a high cognitive burden and introduced significant risk, where small misconfigurations could lead to failed or invalid runs. Instead of guiding users, the system demanded that they adapt to it.

body.text: The approach focused on restructuring the system around user intent rather than system architecture. Instead of exposing all available functionality at once, the experience was redesigned to reveal complexity progressively, allowing users to engage with the system in layers.

sub: The first priority was establishing a clear mental model centered on a natural workflow: select, configure, execute, and review. This would give users an expectation of the flow and fostered confidence through familiarization.  From there, the system was reorganized to support that flow directly, ensuring that each step felt familiar, intentional, and connected.

A containment strategy was introduced to manage complexity. Rather than removing functionality, deeper configuration was isolated into focused overlays, each tied to a specific action. This allowed the main interface to remain clear and navigable while still supporting the full depth of the system when needed.

sections.heading: My Role
body: UX/UI Engineer, Flow Architect.

sections.heading: My Scope
body: End-to-end redesign of the workflow experience, from initial interaction model through high-fidelity design, with close consideration for implementation and system constraints.

sections.heading: The Solution
body: The solution was a complete restructuring of the workflow experience into a centralized, hub-based system that supports a clear and repeatable process. All primary actions were anchored around a single workflow surface, allowing users to select, configure, and execute without losing context.

sub: Configuration was reorganized into a layered model. Core parameters were surfaced directly within the main interface, while secondary and advanced options were moved into scoped overlays. Each overlay was designed with a single responsibility, such as selecting workloads, assigning environments, or modifying pipeline behavior. This eliminated overlap between surfaces and reduced the need for users to search for functionality.

The system now guides users through a defined progression. Selecting a workflow leads naturally into configuration, followed by workload and environment assignment, and ultimately execution. Optional complexity remains accessible, but no longer competes for attention with primary actions.

Run visibility was also significantly improved. A dedicated run history and detail view provides clear feedback on execution status, allowing users to track, inspect, and validate their work without ambiguity. This reinforces trust in the system and reduces the friction associated with debugging or verification.

This project reinforced that complexity in a system is not inherently a problem, but unmanaged complexity is. The original system attempted to expose everything at once, which created confusion rather than empowerment.

body.text: Less is more while keeping robustness
sub: It also highlighted the importance of containment over reduction. Instead of simplifying the system by removing capability, the redesign focused on organizing and isolating it, allowing users to engage with complexity only when necessary.

sections.heading: Outcome
body: The redesigned system transformed a fragmented and cognitively demanding experience into a structured and legible workflow. Users are now able to move through configuration and execution with a clear understanding of where they are, what they are doing, and what comes next.

sections.heading: Challenge and Selection
body: The challenge was reducing cognitive overload within a dense enterprise engineering platform used for complex server component analysis.  The long and short is, the user interface was the front end of software for performing diagnostic tests on various server components across a vast multitude of engineering metrics numbering in the thousands.  The largest stumbling blocks being the need for users to process enormous amounts of technical information through several fragmented workflows.  This created bottomless confusion, navigation fatigue, and horrifying cognitive overload, considering that most users were not even engineers themselves but someone paid to basically push buttons to complete tasks.  I used visualization as my primary design thinking tool because the overriding issue wasn’t a lack of information, it was a lack of order and cohesive orientation throughout the interface’s processes.  More to the point, the user got “lost in the sauce” of trying to stay on course while pushing buttons.  The process would move to the next step and the lack of orientation was confusing and all order would become blurred, to say the very least.

body.text: Visualization was applied through restructuring interface hierarchy, simplifying and consolidating navigation patterns, and setting clear and unmistakable connections between data, flow, and user actions.  More simply put, a straight line was used for a path with the absolute fewest number of operational options.  This proved rather difficult as this led to a need for categorization of metrics.  Someone testing for temperature metrics specifically shouldn’t be inundated with functions for speed testing.  This difficulty was overcome by using a dummied down prototype as proof of concept that grouped a few categories.  User speed increased immediately now that they weren’t having to uncheck several boxes for things they weren’t using.  Conversely, this annoyed the engineering team who now had to build for this.  There’s something to be said about “breaking eggs” and “omelettes” or something but engineers eat Hot Pockets for breakfast.

Moreover, I added modal overlays for items requiring adjustment, such as adding custom scripting, mathematical tweaks, changing metadata and various other actions related to the present workflow.  In my experience I have found that using modal overlays creates a navigation layer without moving the user away from the page they're on.  It essentially layers a temporary page on top, much like using a sticky note that you can hide when you've taken a note.  Users found that having this sort of control without having to navigate away from their present task reduced cognitive overload quite a bit.

sections.heading: Insight and Approach
body: There was an immediate and noticeable change in how users approached the platform, revealing that the primary struggle was not the technical complexity itself, but the fragmented presentation and unclear workflow. Through visualization and clearer interface hierarchy, the platform became easier to navigate, understand, and operate without reducing functionality. Instead of being placed in a maze of disconnected panels, buttons, and toggles that required constant scanning and experimentation, users were guided through a more focused and intentional experience with clear forward and backward progression. The interface shifted from something users had to decipher into something that actively oriented and guided them through their tasks. Additionally, the establishment of a cohesive design system improved scalability and consistency across an entire suite of companion human- and machine-facing software.

groups.desc: The first design was essentially a stop-gap to keep up with the deadline and to try to phase the users into a more user-friendly atmosphere without hitting them over the head with a completely overhauled design. Many of the initial designs were created using PenPot (AMD hadn't yet secured Figma licensure) and our version was Dockerized on a server that was suddenly removed by our maintenance team.  So, yes, these design assets were drawn on paper towels.
groups.label: Web App Layout

items.desc: Rethinking the design overall was met with several challenges.  The first major challenge was establishing a flow that clearly defined a start, a middle, and a finish.  My first thought was, in the politest of terms, the need to figure out how to drink from a firehose without drowning.  That metaphor became a kind of mantra throughout this process, while still keeping in mind that this app was a basic "hack" so that the engineers could test hardware.
User friendliness is a quaint notion when paired with functionality.

When you add all of the moving parts it becomes an even larger compartmentalization challenge.  Since the engineers need to control levels of everything, all of those moving parts are entirely necessary.  That said, tons of those moving poarts were only pertinent to a handful of users at any given moment, and this added to cognitive overload problems. "Overwhelmed" is one of many colorful words that now comes to mind as a user.

sections.heading: Problem
body: People who seek professional organizing services are often already experiencing overwhelm, making it difficult to communicate value, establish trust, and motivate action. The challenge was to design a website that conveyed clarity and calm without adding cognitive or emotional friction.

body.text: The approach focused on reducing cognitive load and establishing trust through clarity, restraint, and intentional structure. The experience was designed to support a gradual decision-making journey, recognizing that users often explore organizing their lives/homes/workplaces/etc., and only later seek professional help when time and cognitive load become overwhelming.

sub: Prioritized understanding how potential clients think and feel when overwhelmed, shaping tone, language, and structure before visual design.
Organized content to guide users through decisions without pressure or distraction.
Designed and built the site to ensure the final experience matched the intent, with attention to performance, accessibility, and consistency.

sections.heading: My Role
body: UX/UI designer, frontend developer, facilitation.

sections.heading: My Scope
body: End-to-end ownership from discovery through implementation

sections.heading: The Solution
body: The solution was a complete website that translated the principles of professional organization into a calm, approachable digital experience. The site balances with clarity, making engagement easy and intuitive.

sub: Content was structured to help users quickly understand services, benefits, and next steps without overwhelming detail
Educational content and examples were used to build trust and demonstrate expertise before asking for commitment.
Spacing, hierarchy, and color were used intentionally to reinforce focus and reduce cognitive load.
The site was designed and implemented as a cohesive system, ensuring the final experience reflected the original intent across devices and interactions.

sections.heading: In Retrospect
body: This project reinforced the importance of meeting people where they are, particularly when they’re already experiencing overwhelm. When a client whose work centers on decluttering is themselves overwhelmed by uncertainty around their website, it becomes clear that clarity, restraint, and pacing are more effective than persuasion or density.

sub: Listening and framing the problem carefully made later design decisions simpler and more consistent.
Reducing visual and informational noise helped communicate credibility and calm more effectively than emphasizing features.
Users often need space to explore and attempt solutions on their own before they’re ready to engage professionally.
Designing and building the site ensured the final experience aligned with the original intent, without dilution.

sections.heading: Outcome
body: The final site provided a clear, calm foundation for the business, aligning its digital presence with the values of organization, focus, and intentional living. The experience supported clearer conversations with potential clients and reduced friction around first contact. This project reflects my facilitation-first approach to UX and frontend work, where clarity and restraint guide both design and decision-making.

projects.title: Web Video Player
projects.subtitle: An Interface For A Video Player Integration

sections.heading: Problem
body: Traditional web video players interrupt the browsing experience by forcing users to navigate away from the primary interface into a dedicated playback environment. This separation breaks context, reduces flexibility in how content is consumed, removes the prospect of engaging with more pieces of content to the user experience, and creates friction when users want to shift between passive listening and active viewing. The challenge was to design a player that allowed continuous interaction with the core page while supporting multiple levels of engagement without disorientation or loss of state.

body.text: The approach focused on maintaining continuity by treating the player as a single persistent object rather than a destination, more of an experiential tool. Instead of routing users to different pages or contexts, the experience was structured around state changes, allowing the player to adapt fluidly between minimized, standard, and fullscreen modes. The system was designed to reveal increased functionality and immersion progressively, while preserving the user’s place within the broader interface. Particular emphasis was placed on spatial and behavioral consistency, ensuring that transitions between states felt like transformations of the same element rather than separate components.

sections.heading: My Role
body: End-to-end interaction design and prototyping, including state modeling, transition behavior, and layout consistency across all player modes.

sections.heading: My Scope
body: End-to-end redesign of the workflow experience, from initial interaction model through high-fidelity design, with close consideration for implementation and system constraints.

sections.heading: The Solution
body: The solution was an adaptive video player that exists as a continuous element within the interface, capable of shifting between multiple states without interrupting the user’s context. From the initial interaction, the player expands from the page into an overlay, maintaining a clear relationship to its origin. From there, users can increase immersion by transitioning into fullscreen or reduce it by collapsing the player into a minimized audio state anchored to the interface.

body.text: Each state preserves core controls and playback continuity, allowing users to move freely between levels of engagement without restarting or reorienting. Transitions were designed to emphasize transformation over replacement, using consistent positioning and scaling to reinforce the perception of a single object evolving in response to user intent. This approach eliminates the need for navigation while supporting a wide range of usage patterns, from focused viewing to background listening.

sections.heading: In Retrospect
body: This project reinforced that continuity is more valuable than separation in media experiences. By avoiding navigation and instead adapting the interface around the user, the system becomes more flexible and less disruptive. It also highlighted the importance of physicality in interaction design, where motion and transformation communicate structure more effectively than static layouts.

body.text: Designing the player as a single entity across all states reduced cognitive overhead and made the experience feel intuitive without requiring explanation. The work demonstrated that users benefit from systems that respond to their level of engagement, rather than forcing them into predefined modes.

sections.heading: Outcome
body: The final design provides a seamless media experience that allows users to control their level of engagement without leaving the central home page. By keeping the player anchored to a consistent “home base,” the system preserves context, reduces cognitive overhead, and eliminates the friction typically introduced by page transitions. Users can move fluidly between passive listening and active viewing while maintaining awareness of their place within the broader interface, enabling multitasking without disruption.

body.text: This continuity improves efficiency and engagement by removing the need to reorient after playback changes, allowing the interface to adapt around the user rather than forcing the user to adapt to it. The result is a more cohesive and responsive experience, where content consumption integrates naturally into the primary workflow instead of interrupting it.

Also a great method for creating a prototype though it can certainly also a bit time intensive as, while not creating every frame of navigation, you're physically aligning on-click overlays for every step.  This SEEMS easy enough until the elements start stacking up and then occasionally, for no identifiable reason, things are suddenly misaligned (auto-snapping and layout anomalies).  The upshot of using this method is that there is far better use of transition animations.

This asset shows the flow of component based navigation.  This is a fantastic method for creating a consistent prototype though it is a bit time intensive as you're essentially creating every frame of navigation, sort of the way an animator creates every frame of a cartoon.

sections.heading: Problem
body: Furniture shopping on mobile is often fragmented and overwhelming, with cluttered navigation, unclear product differentiation, and friction in moving from browsing to decision-making. Users struggle to explore styles, compare options, and confidently select products without cognitive overload.

body.text: The approach focused on simplifying exploration and decision-making through clear structure, visual hierarchy, and progressive disclosure.

sub: Centered the experience around how users browse furniture—visually first, analytically second—prioritizing inspiration before specification.
Created a straightforward category system (Living Rooms, Kitchens, Bedrooms, etc.) to reduce friction and support intuitive movement through the app.
Designed flows that allow users to move from broad categories → product grids → detailed views without disruption.

sections.heading: My Role
body: UX/UI designer, product thinker.

sections.heading: My Scope
body: End-to-end design from concept to high-fidelity prototype

sections.heading: The Solution
body: The solution is a mobile-first furniture shopping experience that balances inspiration with clarity, allowing users to browse, evaluate, and select products with minimal friction.

sub: Category-based navigation paired with consistent product grids enables fast scanning and predictable interaction patterns.
Large imagery and clean layouts prioritize the product itself, reducing reliance on dense text.
Each product view highlights key differentiators (style, color options, naming) without overwhelming the user.

Streamlined sign-in and account creation screens reduce barriers to engagement.  I DID want to highlight the iterative process so I therefore created a way to see the overall evolution of aestehtics/functionality/etc. (Create Account: OG design vs. revised styling).
Consistent spacing, muted color palette, and simple typography maintain focus and reduce cognitive load.
Users don’t need novelty when making purchasing decisions—they need confidence and ease.
Furniture is inherently visual, so the interface succeeds when it gets out of the way.
Repeating patterns across categories and product views reduces learning time and increases comfort.
Keeping the feature set focused allowed the core experience (browse → evaluate → select) to feel polished and intentional.

sections.heading: Outcome
body: The prototype demonstrates a clean, scalable foundation for a mobile furniture shopping experience that prioritizes usability, clarity, and visual engagement. The design reduces friction in product discovery and supports confident decision-making, reflecting a UX approach grounded in structure, restraint, and user intent.

sections.heading: Problem
body: In my work as an app developer at Accenture, our human resources department contacted me needing a tool to redact sensitive items on pdf documents in a destructive way that could not be reversed.  Up to this point their process involved printing all of the pdfs, redacting them with a black marker and rescanning everything and was VERY time intensive creating weeks of work over the fiscal year.

body.text: The approach for this required examining how pdfs are handled in various pdf platforms (Adobe, Microsoft, et al).  The simplest approach was to create an overlay that I could create redactions on and then save the whole thing as a new pdf.

sub: Centered the experience around how users browse furniture—visually first, analytically second—prioritizing inspiration before specification.
Designed and built the site to ensure the final experience matched the intent, with attention to performance, accessibility, and consistency.

sections.heading: My Role
body: UX/UI designer, developer, facilitation

sections.heading: My Scope
body: End-to-end ownership from discovery through implementation

sections.heading: The Solution
body: The solution was a complete web app (html, Javascript, css)  that allowed the user to simply load the pdfs into the interface, draw redaction shapes onto them (click-drag), and export them as new pdfs while leaving the original pdfs unaltered.  More than anything, leveraging Javascript (web functionality) and a very commonly and widely used Javascript library (pdf.js).  Moreover, I implemented 4 distinct functions into the app.

sub: The user loads a pdf, makes redactions, exports the new pdf leaving the original unaltered. Search function:  This function allows for a keyword search inside of the interface, highlighting keywords as needed.
The user has the option to save the redactions they have made into a template that can later be added to other pdfs as needed via the user interface.

The user loads multiple pdfs into the interface and then loads a redaction template onto all of them.  This is a one and done process as many of the pdfs they were redacting were created from common forms from the human resources files and therefore created commonly structured pdfs.  This facilitated a “1 template fits all” solution drastically reducing work.
Spacing, hierarchy, and color were used intentionally to reinforce focus and reduce cognitive load.
The redactions are irreversible because they become part of the document and are neither an overlay of it nor a black highlight.
The site was designed and implemented as a cohesive system, ensuring the final experience reflected the original intent across devices and interactions.

body.text: This project moved the ball forward for the client, dramatically reducing the time required to actually redact and save sensitive files.  As a result of the destructive nature of the tool there were improved levels of assurance that they were getting exactly what was required of the app.

sections.heading: Outcome
body: The final product happily surprised the client owing to its simplicity in use, function, and design.  As a UX problem the design was relatively straight-forward.  The true challenge of it lay in its complication of function (many buttons!!!).  This primary issue was overcome in maintaining good UX, labeling things in a concise way and holding fast to my belief in not navigating users away from the products primary purpose.  Also, keeping the interface in a process ladder format whereby all steps occur from top to bottom was an important way to solve for cognitive overload in a rather complicated process.
